snippet.title: Police Are Investigating a Large Burning Cross at Grant Park
snippet.description:
A large, burning cross was discovered at Grant Park on Tuesday afternoon, and police said they are investigating how it ended up there and the motive behind it.

Video taken by a motorist shows the wooden cross engulfed in bright orange flames as it leans against a tree in Grant Park, a popular area near Lake Michigan. The Chicago Fire Department confirmed the flaming object was a cross, and said officials put out the fire.

Chicago Police said there were no reports of injuries and that they are investigating the motive and circumstances around the “object on fire.“

While the motive behind the burning cross was not immediately clear, cross burnings in the U.S. have historically been seen as “symbols of hate” that are “inextricably intertwined with the history of the Ku Klux Klan,” according to a 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision written by the late Justice Sandra Day O’Connor. The justices ruled that the First Amendment allows bans on cross burnings only when they are intended to intimidate because the action “is a particularly virulent form of intimidation.”

snippet.title: WWII Fighter Planes and Secret Weapons That Changed History
snippet.description:
Soar into the untold stories of World War II aircraft, from the legendary P-51 Mustang to the fearsome German ME 262 jet fighter, and the pilots who changed history.

Discover how daring engineering and fierce aerial combat shaped the outcome of World War II. This video dives deep into the evolution of iconic planes like the F6F Hellcat, P-47 Thunderbolt, Bf 109, FW 190 DORA, and the revolutionary ME 262. Learn how turbo superchargers, bio-inspired wing designs, and disposable fuel tanks gave the Allies a critical edge. Relive the high-stakes dogfights over D-Day, the strategic bombing campaigns, and the intense carrier battles in the Pacific.

You’ll meet the heroic Tuskegee Airmen, whose Red Tails protected bombers over Nazi Germany and broke barriers at home. Witness the terror of the V-2 rocket, Germany’s desperate technological gamble, and see how both Allied and Axis engineers raced to perfect new weapons. Experience the challenges of torpedo bombing runs against the mighty Musashi, and the ingenuity behind radio navigation that brought lost pilots home across the Pacific. The video highlights not just the machines, but the pilots’ personal stories, triumphs, and sacrifices that defined the air war in WWII.

Perfect for aviation enthusiasts, history buffs, and anyone fascinated by the game-changing technology and heroism that shaped the fate of nations.

snippet.description:

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on the history of medieval period and Franks continues with a video on how the history of the Lombards. Before Lombardy became a region of Italy, the Lombards were a roaming warrior people whose origin story mixed myth, migration, politics, and war. This video follows their rise from the legendary “long-beards” of the Winnils to one of the most important Germanic kingdoms of the early Middle Ages. We trace how a small tribal coalition entered Roman records, settled in Pannonia, fought the Heruli and Gepids, and served the Eastern Roman Empire before turning against it. Under King Alboin, the Lombards invaded a devastated Italy in 568, seized Milan and Pavia, and carved out a kingdom among the ruins of Rome. But conquest brought instability: murder, autonomous dukes, Byzantine resistance, religious change, and a society built around warriors, law, honour, and hierarchy. The story then turns to the 8th century, when Lombard expansion threatened Rome itself, forcing the Pope to seek protection from the rising Carolingian Franks. From Alboin’s bloody legend to Pippin’s invasions and the birth of the Papal States, this is the story of how the Lombards reshaped Italy—and why their kingdom could not survive Frankish power. It is a transformation story linking Rome’s collapse, barbarian migration, medieval state-building, and the rise of Charlemagne’s world in medieval Europe.

snippet.title: The Real 'American Me' Was the Most Dangerous Gang Story Ever Filmed
snippet.description:
On March 25, 1992, just 12 days after American Me premiered in theaters, a gunman walked up behind 53-year-old Charles “Charlie Brown” Manriquez in Ramona Gardens and fired 3 shots into his back. 2 months later, 49-year-old grandmother Ana Lizarraga, the film’s most beloved consultant, was ambushed and gunned down outside her home. The movie meant to scare kids away from gang life had become a death warrant.

In this deep-dive documentary, we uncover the real story behind Edward James Olmos’s 1992 cult classic American Me and the four real men who inspired its most iconic characters.

What you will learn:
- The true biography of Rodolfo “Cheyenne” Cadena, the 16-year-old killer from Bakersfield who became the architect of La Eme
- How Joe “Pegleg” Morgan, a Croatian-American bank robber, became the first non-Mexican godfather of the Mexican Mafia
- The legend of Jap Mike Kudo, the Japanese American who shattered every rule of gang membership
- Why former hitman Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza warned Olmos about the contract on his life and was ignored
- The exact scenes in American Me that the Mexican Mafia considered an unforgivable insult to Cadena’s memory
- The 1992 federal extortion indictment that named Edward James Olmos as a victim of Joe Morgan
- The $500,000 lawsuit filed by Morgan’s widow after his 1993 death from liver cancer

Key figures and timeline: 
The Mexican Mafia formed at Deuel Vocational Institution around 1957. Cadena arrived in 1959 at age 16 after a fatal stabbing. By 1961, the founding members were transferred to San Quentin, where the gang exploded into power. Cadena was murdered on December 17, 1972 in Palm Hall, Chino. Joe Morgan died November 8, 1993 at California State Prison, Corcoran. The film American Me was released March 13, 1992, triggering at least 2 confirmed killings and dozens more alleged hits.

Why this story matters today: 
The Mexican Mafia still controls Sureño street gangs across the American Southwest from inside solitary confinement units. The American Me killings prove that a prison gang formed in a juvenile facility nearly 70 years ago can still reach into the free world and silence anyone who tells its story wrong.

snippet.title: They Created the Mafia — Then the Next Generation Slaughtered Them
snippet.description:
They were the original Mafia bosses — and they refused to change.

Before Lucky Luciano modernized the American Mafia, a powerful old generation ruled by Sicilian tradition, superstition, and bloodline loyalty. They were known as the Mustache Petes — old-world gangsters who brought medieval codes into a modern America they barely understood.

This video tells the true story of how these bosses built the Mafia… and why the next generation destroyed them.

We dive deep into the lives, rivalries, and fatal mistakes of the most important Mustache Petes in Mafia history, including:

🔹 Salvatore Maranzano — the self-styled Roman general who modeled the Mafia after Julius Caesar’s legions, blind to the modern criminal world forming beneath him
🔹 Ignazio “The Wolf” Lupo — a Black Hand terror whose reputation relied as much on superstition and fear as violence
🔹 Joe “The Boss” Masseria — whose slow, old-world leadership ended with a legendary betrayal over a card game
🔹 Gaetano Reina — caught between loyalty to tradition and the rising Young Turks
🔹 Nicola Gentile — the old-world mediator whose obsession with etiquette stalled business and fueled war
🔹 Stefano Magaddino — an early Mustache Pete survivor who quietly adapted when others couldn’t

Through real historical accounts, FBI records, and firsthand memoirs, this documentary shows how superstition lost to strategy, how tradition lost to profit, and how the Mafia’s founders were ultimately slaughtered by the empire they created.

This is not Hollywood.
This is the real birth of the modern American Mafia.

snippet.title: The Real Nucky Johnson: The Crime Boss Atlantic City Forgot
snippet.description:

What you’ll learn in this documentary:
• How a 25-year-old sheriff became the most powerful political boss in New Jersey

 • Why Nucky personally walked Al Capone through the Boardwalk after the Breakers Hotel refused him a room
 • How the National Crime Syndicate and the Commission were actually born on the Atlantic City Boardwalk

snippet.title: How the Mob Took Over Philadelphia — And Destroyed Itself
snippet.description:
For decades, the Philadelphia Mafia operated in near silence. While New York and Chicago grabbed headlines with public shootouts and infamous gangsters, Philadelphia’s underworld was built differently — through restraint, political influence, labor control, and quiet corruption embedded deep within the city’s institutions. This documentary traces the true history of how the Mafia took over Philadelphia, from early Italian immigration and Black Hand extortion, through Prohibition and the rise of organized crime, to the long, disciplined reign of Angelo Bruno, the man known as The Gentle Don. Under Bruno, the Philadelphia crime family thrived by avoiding attention, controlling unions, construction, gambling, and Atlantic City’s casino boom — all while maintaining peace on the streets. But when Bruno was murdered in 1980, everything changed. What followed was a decade of brutal internal warfare under Nicodemo “Little Nicky” Scarfo, featuring car-trunk executions, nail-bomb assassinations, drug trafficking, and unprecedented violence that finally drew intense federal scrutiny. Using RICO laws, wiretaps, and insider testimony, prosecutors dismantled what had once been one of the most quietly powerful criminal organizations in America. This is not a Hollywood version of the Mafia. This is the documented rise — and violent collapse — of Philadelphia’s real criminal empire.

The Black Hand and early extortion rackets
Prohibition and the consolidation of power

RICO prosecutions and the fall of the Philadelphia Mob

snippet.title: The Real Danny Greene Was the Most Dangerous Man Behind 'Kill the Irishman'
snippet.description:
October 6, 1977. A car bomb in a Lyndhurst, Ohio parking lot ends the life of Danny Greene, the Celtic Club founder who survived 7 professional assassination attempts and humiliated the entire Cleveland Mafia for nearly a decade. What the Hollywood film “Kill the Irishman” couldn’t show you is darker, stranger, and far more documented than the cinematic version.
In this deep dive investigation, we unpack the real story of Danny Greene, the Marine turned longshoreman turned FBI top-echelon informant who built a criminal empire on Cleveland’s east side while simultaneously feeding intelligence to federal agents for 13 years.

What you’ll learn in this episode:
- How an Irish orphan from Collinwood took on an entire La Cosa Nostra family and won
- The exact mechanics of Greene’s “tax” on Cleveland’s bookmakers, generating $8,000 to $15,000 a week
- The full timeline of all 7 failed assassination attempts between 1975 and 1977
- The murder of Shondor Birns and how Greene killed his own mentor
- How hitman Ray Ferritto’s arrest triggered the largest organized crime prosecution in Ohio history
- The chain reaction that produced 22 federal convictions and destroyed the Cleveland crime family permanently
- How underboss Angelo Lonardo’s cooperation helped Rudy Giuliani destroy the Five Families

Key Figures: 
Danny Greene, James “Jack White” Licavoli, John Nardi, Shondor Birns, Ray Ferritto, Angelo Lonardo, John Scalish
Timeline: 
1933 (Greene’s birth) — 1964 (becomes FBI informant) — 1975 (first bomb survived) — October 6, 1977 (Greene killed) — 1982 (Cleveland family destroyed)

Why this story matters in 2026: 
Danny Greene’s case remains the single most consequential informant operation in American organized crime history. The intelligence pipeline that began with his 1964 cooperation ultimately fed into the 1986 Commission Trial that broke the Five Families. Every modern federal RICO prosecution traces a line back to Cleveland.

Born Francesco Raffaele Nitto in Italy and raised in poverty in Brooklyn, Frank Nitti arrived in Chicago during Prohibition and quickly became Al Capone's right-hand man. As "The Enforcer," he orchestrated brutal hits, managed the Outfit's massive bootlegging, gambling, and extortion rackets, and kept the syndicate running like a ruthless business empire.
When Capone went to prison in 1931 for tax evasion, Nitti stepped up as boss – transforming the mob into a more sophisticated operation focused on labor unions, Hollywood shakedowns, and millions in untouchable profits. But as federal pressure mounted in 1943 – including indictments for extorting movie studios – Nitti's world crumbled. On March 19, 1943, he walked drunkenly to a railroad track in a Chicago suburb and took his own life rather than face prison.

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on early modern warfare where we talk about the evolution of the Star Fort, the genius behind its design and Fort Mchenry. When cannon fire made medieval castles obsolete, European engineers answered with one of the most important military designs in history: the bastion fort. This video traces the rise of the low, angular “star fort,” from Renaissance Italy and the Trace Italienne to the great fortress systems of the Netherlands, Habsburg frontier, and Vauban’s France. We explain why tall walls failed, how angled bastions eliminated blind spots, and why siege warfare became a deadly contest of mathematics, trenches, artillery, and engineering. Then the story crosses the Atlantic to Baltimore, where Fort McHenry turned European fortress theory into American coastal defence. Built on Whetstone Point to guard Baltimore Harbor, its pentagonal bastions, dry moat, glacis, and heavy guns faced their defining test during the War of 1812. After burning Washington, the British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry for 25 hours, but the fort held, the flag still flew, and Francis Scott Key found the image that became The Star-Spangled Banner. From Italian city-states to the Chesapeake, this is the story of how star forts changed warfare—and how one American bastion became a national symbol of resistance, engineering, and survival under fire, remembered long after the guns fell silent in 1814 and beyond forever.

snippet.title: The Longest-Reigning Mafia Boss You’ve Never Heard Of
snippet.description:
Meet Stefano “The Undertaker” Magaddino. While Al Capone made headlines and John Gotti chased cameras, Magaddino sat quietly in a funeral home in Western New York, pulling the strings of the American Mafia for over half a century.

In this deep-dive documentary, we explore the incredible true story of the Buffalo Crime Family’s "Boss of Bosses." From his secret role as the "Central Banker" for the 1930s Castellammarese War to his sprawling Lewiston fortress where he watched the Canadian border through a telescope, Magaddino’s reign was built on one principle: Patience is Power.
In this video, you’ll discover:

-The "Undertaker" Strategy: How he used funeral hearses to move millions in illicit cargo across the Peace Bridge.
-The "Mafia UN": Why Buffalo became a safe haven for international fugitives and the French Connection heroin ring.
-The FBI’s "Big Ear": The shocking declassified tapes from the "Stefano Bug" that captured the Don’s private rants and internal betrayals.
-The $500,000 Suitcase: The secret stash hidden under a bed that sparked a bloody mutiny in the Buffalo underworld.
-The "Dying Don" Act: How Magaddino pioneered the oxygen-mask-and-wheelchair defense to stay out of prison until his death in 1974.
-Witness the history of a man who survived the "Banana Wars," outlasted the Five Families of New York, and proved that the most dangerous man in the room is the one you never notice.
"He didn't need to be famous to be powerful—he needed only to be unremarked."

snippet.title: Why this Mob Boss Only Lasted 359 Days
snippet.description:
"They call me the Chicken Man..."

In the early morning of March 15, 1981, a massive explosion rocked South Philadelphia, shattering the windows of Zesto’s Pizza and ending the life of Philip "The Chicken Man" Testa. He had been the boss of the Philadelphia Mafia for exactly 359 days.

In this deep dive, we explore the rise and violent fall of a man who tried to hold onto the "old ways" in a world that had already moved on to fire and blood. From his humble beginnings at United Poultry on Christian Street to the sophisticated remote-controlled nail bomb that tore his front porch—and the family—apart, this is the story of the shortest and most pivotal reign in American Mafia history.

In this video, we cover:
-The Power Vacuum: How the assassination of the "Gentle Don," Angelo Bruno, forced Philip Testa onto a throne he couldn't keep.
-The 3:15 AM Pronouncement: Setting the record straight on the timeline of the St. Agnes Hospital emergency room.
-The Tovex Conspiracy: Why the plotters used a construction-grade nail bomb instead of a traditional hitman.
-The Casella Coup: The internal betrayal by Peter Casella and the triggerman, Rocco Marinucci.

The Legacy of Fire: How Testa’s death paved the way for the paranoid "Murder Machine" of Nicky Scarfo and the eventual collapse of the Philly Mob.

snippet.title: The Real War Dogs: Inside the Most Insane Arms Deal in The U.S. History
snippet.description:
Two Miami Beach kids. A strip mall office above a laundromat. A $298 million Pentagon contract to arm the Afghan National Army with 100 million rounds of ammunition. This is the true story of Efraim Diveroli and David Packouz, the founders of AEY Incorporated, who beat Lockheed Martin and General Dynamics at the Pentagon’s own bidding game, then nearly armed an entire foreign military with 40-year-old rotting Chinese ammunition smuggled through Albania.

In this deep-dive investigation, you’ll learn:
• How Efraim Diveroli, at just 21 years old, exploited the Federal Business Opportunities website like an eBay loophole
 • The exact mechanics of how AEY undercut major defense contractors by $53 million
 • Why Chinese-made ammunition was illegal under U.S. law and how AEY allegedly repackaged it in cardboard boxes to hide its origin
 • The role of Albanian businessman Kosta Trebicka and the secret phone recordings that brought everything down
 • How New York Times reporter C.J. Chivers exposed the entire operation in March 2008
 • The mysterious mountain road death of the only witness who could have named names
 • The 71 federal counts, prison sentences, and how the Pentagon’s entire small-business contracting system was overhauled

Key figures: 
Efraim Diveroli (CEO, AEY Inc.), David Packouz (Vice President), Kosta Trebicka (Albanian supplier), C.J. Chivers (NYT investigative reporter), Senator Carl Levin (Senate Armed Services Committee).

Timeline: 
2005 founding of AEY operations, January 2007 contract award, March 2008 NYT exposé, September 2008 death of Kosta Trebicka, 2009 federal sentencing.

This story matters because it exposed the dangerous gap in how the U.S. military vets the people who arm its allies. The reforms that followed AEY shaped every Pentagon small business contract written in the years since. It’s also the story behind the Hollywood film “War Dogs,” though the truth is far darker than the movie ever showed.

snippet.title: Why the FBI Failed to Take Down the Mafia For Decades
snippet.description:
For decades, the American Mafia operated in plain sight — powerful, organized, and largely untouchable. While local police, journalists, and Senate investigators warned of a nationwide criminal syndicate, the FBI’s most powerful leader refused to fully acknowledge it.

Why?

This documentary-style deep dive uncovers how J. Edgar Hoover’s priorities, legal roadblocks, political corruption, and the Mafia’s own code of silence allowed organized crime to thrive for decades — until a series of shocks changed everything.

From the 1957 Apalachin meeting that exposed the national Mafia network, to Hoover’s long denial, the Valachi hearings, the creation of RICO, the rise of wiretaps and witness protection, and the eventual takedown of the Mafia’s top leadership, this is the full story of why the FBI failed for so long — and how they finally won.

Featuring:

The truth behind J. Edgar Hoover and organized crime
Why the FBI focused on communism instead of the Mafia
How corruption protected mob bosses
The legal limits that made prosecutions nearly impossible
The turning points that shattered omertà
How RICO, wiretaps, and informants changed history
The rise and fall of figures like Joseph Valachi, Paul Castellano, and John Gotti

This isn’t a movie myth or gangster fantasy — it’s the real, documented history of America’s longest war against organized crime.

snippet.title: How Illegal Drugs Are Smuggled Around The World — From Cocaine To Steroids | How Crime Works
snippet.description:
Andrew Pritchard was a major UK drug smuggler who orchestrated the trafficking of $130 million worth of cocaine from the Caribbean to Europe. He started by smuggling drugs in concealed suitcases for the UK club scene before escalating to massive shipping container operations. Despite being acquitted in a high-profile 2004 customs bust, Pritchard was ultimately arrested after a high-speed chase in 2013 and sentenced to 15 years in Belmarsh prison. Since his release, he has authored two biographies, "Urban Smuggler" and "Empire of Dirt," and runs the AP Foundation, an ex-offender charity dedicated to steering youth away from crime.

William Roger Reaves is a former pilot, boat captain, and prolific drug smuggler who flew massive loads of cocaine and marijuana from Colombia to the US for the Medellín Cartel. An associate of infamous figures like Barry Seal (played by Tom Cruise in "American Made") and Pablo Escobar, Reaves spent over 33 years imprisoned across five different countries, including Mexico, Australia, and the US. In 2016, he published a memoir from prison, "Smuggler," and he now lives in Santa Barbara, California.

Chet Sandhu is a former smuggler who trafficked an estimated $50 million worth of illegal steroids. In the mid-1990s, he operated a massive trafficking network that sourced steroids from Karachi, Pakistan, and smuggled them into the UK via routes including the Netherlands, France, and Spain by bribing airport security. Following his arrest, Sandhu was sentenced to serve over four years in the infamous Fontcalent correctional facility in Alicante, Spain. He has since authored two books, "From King of Karachi to Lockdown in the Costa Del Crime" and "Self-Made, Dues Paid," and he now runs a CBD company.

David McMillan is a British-Australian former drug smuggler who trafficked an estimated $17 million worth of heroin internationally. Between the early 1980s and 2012, McMillan was arrested multiple times for smuggling heroin through Southeast and Central Asia to markets in the US and Europe. Since leaving the trade, he has worked as a public speaker and authored two books, "Escape" and "Unforgiving Destiny."

Owen Hanson is a former University of Southern California football player who went from smuggling steroids in college to running the ODOG Enterprise, a massive illegal sports betting operation. After expanding into cartel-backed money laundering and drug trafficking, Hanson was arrested by the FBI in 2015 and sentenced to over 21 years in federal prison. He served nine years in prison following his arrest and forfeited $5 million in assets. He is the author of "The California Kid: From USC Golden Boy to International Drug Kingpin" and the subject of the Prime Video docuseries "Cocaine Quarterback."

snippet.title: The Shocking Truth About Victorian Workhouses and Family Secrets
snippet.description:
Step inside the haunting world of the Victorian Workhouse - an institution that shaped millions of British lives and left a legacy still felt today.

Discover the untold stories of families like those of Felicity Kendall, Brian Cox, and Barbara Taylor Bradford, as they uncover their ancestors’ experiences inside the notorious workhouses of Britain. This documentary traces how the workhouse system, designed to punish and stigmatize the poor, forced desperate families apart and created an underclass defined by shame and secrecy. From the heartbreak of illegitimate births and forced child removals to the hard-won triumphs of those who escaped, you’ll see how workhouse life evolved from cruelty to the beginnings of modern social welfare.

Follow real journeys through original archives and moving personal accounts as we reveal how workhouses not only provided shelter but also enforced harsh moral codes, separated children from parents, and cast a shadow over generations. Learn about the migration schemes that sent thousands of vulnerable children overseas, and see how the resilience of those affected helped shape the modern welfare state. With keywords like Victorian workhouse history, family secrets, child migration, and the origins of the NHS, this video is a must-watch for anyone interested in social history and genealogy.
